If some, like anatomical connectivity, are not critical, then they obfuscates the main findings and worsens the overall readability of the paper (which is very good, but a bit long) and could be removed or moved to a supplementary figure showing unequivocally in what ways it does (not) constrain the model. It is somewhat acknowledged in the paper that the main driver of the findings is the gradient of recurrent excitation (“As a matter of fact, the relevant parameter here is the strength of synaptic excitation that varies across cortical space, in the form of a macroscopic gradient”), but this is not very clear at times. Again, if this is indeed the case, less emphasis should be given to the anatomical “constraints” and instead the relevant feature should be spelled out clearly and early on (in the abstract and intro)

Simplified model.

It is not very clear what we gain with this model, if not to show that with homogeneous coupling (instead of heterogeneous from experimental data, see above) similar findings are achieved. The model is motivated by “The above model, albeit a simplification of real brain circuits, includes several biologically realistic features, which makes it difficult to identify essential ingredients for the emergence of distributed WM.” This seems a good reason to remove the “biological constraints” from the “full model” (see above). Additionally, because of where this model is introduced in the paper, it becomes unclear when the simplified or the full model is used in the following figures. This could be improved if the simplified model was introduced only in the supplementary material or in a subpanel with a clear title. At a minimum, all captions should say if the full/simplified model were used.

Previous experimental literature.

Overall we feel that several studies were not properly considered. For instance, Guo et al., Nature is not cited properly, nor discussed. Note for example that also in this paper there was a model – in addition to clear empirical evidence – with different areas and similar concepts as the ones that are explored here.

Likewise, both "Cortical information flow during flexible sensorimotor decisions" Markus Siegel et al., Nature and also Panichello and Buschman, Nature were not considered in this study. In both studies, they recorded from several areas across the hierarchy (from visual cortex to PFC) during WM and DM, so they seem to be extremely relevant, especially to constrain the model further in future studies. For example, Panichello and Buschman show clear WM codes in V4, not present in the current model. Another example: "We observed (…) a sharp binary jump of activity, areas like LIP exhibited a more gradual ramping activity, resembling temporal accumulation of information in decision-making(Shadlen and Newsome, 2001)". Siegel et al., Science show very convincing evidence that this is actually not the case and the model does not seem to match the latencies reported here.

Of course, this mismatch between data and model is not very important and it does not reduce the value of the current model, but the authors should consider toning down claims like "strong agreement with" or "an excellent agreement with a large body of data, from decades of monkey neurophysiological" which occur throughout the study. The model is a great proof of concept that provides several important insights, but it is far from being in "strong agreement" with what happens in the brain.

Somatosensory WM.

Relatedly, the authors perform an experiment that simulates "somatosensory WM". While the question as to which areas trigger the global attractor is interesting and would deserve to be explored further, the way this is framed (i.e. studying different WM modalities) is misleading and should be adapted. Figure2—figure supplement2 shows that the same global attractor is engaged irrespectively of which area is stimulated. The evidence points otherwise (see Christophel et al., 2017). For example Figure2—figure supplement2 shows persistent activity in IT, which would not be expected for somatosensory WM?

Inactivations.

It would be nice to have a schematic of when this inactivation is performed (which we think it is throughout the trial), like in FIGURE 7. It seems that the point made in fig6 C needs the areas to be silenced in the opposite direction (ie hierarchical order) to be conclusive. Figure F seems important, as well as the result in G, but it is very confusing. We would consider simplifying it to show more clearly the relevant features/points made. Again: how much of the findings (in particular the "bowtie" analyses) here depend on the "anatomical constraints" is unclear.

"which is in agreement with classical prefrontal lesion studies(Curtis and D'esposito, 2004)" The cited paper does not do what the authors did in the model. This line should be removed of better explained

"In some cases, inactivating specific areas might even lead to a disinhibition of other areas and to a general reinforcement of the attractor". Again, unclear why this is. Does this depend on gradient of recurrent excitation, hierarchy location or anatomical connectivity?

Relationship with other mechanisms of working memory.

This paragraph, while important, seems a bit incomplete in the current form. In particular the part where activity-silent is discussed. The results presented here seem to depend strongly on the persistent activity hypothesis of working memory. Does it make sense to think about distributed attractors through short-term plasticity? The relationship with silent activity does not seem straightforward and this discussion failed to illuminate it.

In the next paragraph, the authors say "This also means that silent activity periods associated with silent WM (Masse et al., 2019; Mongillo et al., 2008; Stokes, 2015)could also be due to distributed WM effects. Optogenetic inactivations could be used to test this result." This is an interesting idea, but could be expanded a bit more. Intriguingly, the authors cite papers (Masse et al., 2019; Mongillo et al.,) of local circuits with actual activity-siment mechanism. Instead, the author should cite empirical evidence of silent periods, of which the model proposed here offers an alternative view. For example: Wolff et al., Nature Neuroscience (Human occipital cortex), Barbosa et al., Nature Neuroscience (monkey PFC) and Akrami et al., Nature, (rodent PPC) etc.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

I am not suggesting that the authors overhaul their model and start over. But a re-write (and some changing of terms, see below) would serve them well. I would encourage the authors to consider changing the tone of manuscript so that it doesn't come across as if persistent attractors are state-of-the-art thinking about working memory. I suggest a more up-front acknowledging of the newer developments (as opposed to a single paragraph near the end of the Discussion) and that their work will focus on mechanisms that allow average activity to remain elevated. Right now, it reads as if "persistent activity" is everything, with a disclaimer near the end.

Finally, I encourage the authors to not use the term "persistent activity" (try elevated or sustained elevated activity or just "delay activity"). As noted above, there is evidence against persistent activity. But more to the point, there is little or no evidence for persistent activity. Virtually all of the work purporting such evidence averaged neural activity across multiple trials. Across-trial averaging masks more complex dynamics like gaps of no spiking. One cannot conclude persistent firing from averaged data. It can only be addressed in real time at the single trial level. Also, there is a no definition of "persistent". Is it a spike every 5 ms? Every 10 ms? Every 100 ms? Using a term like "persistent activity" when it is not well defined and for which there is little direct evidence muddies the waters and does not do a service to the field.

Other comments:

One cannot help but wonder how the hierarchical trends discussed here relate to other hierarchical trends. For example, there is a gradual progression from sensory-related activity to task-relevant activity as one ascends the hierarchy. Or the greater mixed selectivity in higher cortex. Maybe those are separate issues. But if the authors have any insights into how their model contributes to them, it would certainly add value to their manuscript.

Page 4: "LIP exhibited a more gradual ramping activity, resembling temporal accumulation of information in decision making (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001)". Again, this was state-of-the-art like a decade ago. It ignores more recent work by Pillow, Shenoy, and others showing that the ramp-up is not gradual. When examined on the single-trial level, the activity is instead a series of discrete state changes. This does not take anything away from the elegant and important work of Shadlen and Newsome, without which the newer work would not have been possible. But, again, by focusing on older, not newer, work, the authors are not giving a full account of where we are in 2021.

[Editors’ note: further revisions were suggested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Mechanisms of distributed working memory in a large-scale network of macaque neocortex" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Tirin Moore (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:

Reviewers were largely satisfied with the revised manuscript with one exception. They were concerned about the discussion of the role of plasticity in Attractor and Activity-Silent models (lines 559-566). It was felt that the work referred to in the Wang recent review which showed more spiking activity during manipulation of working memory, did not rule out synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, it was pointed out that Activity-Silent models also predict that spiking may be used to "ping" the network and read out the memories. In this case, the role of plasticity is to HELP the spiking, not to replace it.

To address this concern, this section should be modified. One option would be to provide clear evidence that synaptic plasticity only holds for Activity-Silent models and is not required by the attractor models. This can be done by citing specific references with the appropriate simulations/data or by providing new simulations/data.

Alternatively, this paragraph should be modified by allowing short-term plasticity to play a role in both types of models.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

With most of my initial concerns addressed and the inclusion of interesting, new simulations, I fully support the publication of the manuscript in the current form.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors' revisions are mostly adequate.

However, the statements that activity-silent models " (1) it cannot filter out distractors that occur later in time than behavioral relevant stimuli, (2) it does not have a severely limited capacity (a characteristic of working memory) and (3) it is incapable of internal manipulation of information" is not true.

The activity-silent models can explain all of this. Synaptic weight changes are driven and refreshed by spiking. Thus, they have the same features and same control as attractor-state models. 1. Distractors can be filtered out by controlling spiking. 2. They do have a severe capacity limitation due to limitations in the spiking refresh rate. Multiple memories cannot be in the active state at the same time. That leads to capacity limitations. 3. Manipulation of WM is achieved by controlling spiking episodes, just like the attractor-state models.

The issue is that in testing the activity-silent models, the author has shifted too much of the burden to synapses alone. That is a misrepresentation of the activity-silent models. It is easy to refute a model if one makes a straw model of it. In the activity-silent models, synapses don't do everything. The help activity by briefly carrying the memories between spiking. That is why they are also referred to as "synaptic attractor" models. Because they also involve attractor states, they have many of the same features and mechanisms as attractor-state models. As a wise colleague recently said, the attractor-state and synaptic-attractor models are more similar than different. The characterization that the former can explain a variety of WM phenomena but the latter cannot is not accurate.

I think this is a valuable review. It is well-written. Attractor dynamics are indeed important and the review offers important insights. But surely these insights can be offered with misrepresenting other models.

claims.claim: In distributed WM networks, an area can recover encoded selective information once inhibitory pulse is removed.
claims.source: On the other hand, silencing an area like 9/46d will slightly affect the sustained activity in other areas (such as 8B) in a network strongly relying on distributed WM (Figure 7C, middle row). However, area 9/46d will be able to recover the encoded selective information once the inhibitory pulse is removed, due to the strong interaction between cortical areas during the delay period.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C middle row.

claims.claim: Distributed WM activity patterns can be shut down with excitatory input targeting inhibitory populations of areas high in the hierarchy.
claims.source: We therefore explore in our model whether more spatially selective signals can shut down distributed patterns of activity. In spite of their robustness to sensory distractors as discussed above, we find that distributed WM activity patterns can be shut down with an excitatory input targeting inhibitory populations of areas high in the hierarchy.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as a finding from the model.

claims.claim: A visually evoked distributed WM attractor can be deactivated by delivering excitatory input to inhibitory populations in the top four areas of the hierarchy.
claims.source: Figure 7C (bottom row) shows how a visually evoked distributed WM attractor is deactivated when we deliver excitatory input to the inhibitory populations in the top four areas of the hierarchy (9/46v, 9/46d, F7 and 8B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C bottom row.

claims.claim: Distributed WM attractors can be controlled and deactivated by localized inhibition to a small set of frontal areas.
claims.source: Therefore, in spite of engaging cortical areas across all four lobes, distributed WM attractors can be controlled and deactivated by localized inhibition to a small set of frontal areas.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Localized WM networks can be distracted with stimuli similar or even weaker than the minimum cue input strength required to encode a WM pattern.
claims.source: Overall, we found that localized WM networks can be distracted with stimuli similar or even weaker than the minimum cue input strength required to encode a WM pattern, while effective distractors need to be about three times as strong in the case of distributed WM networks (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: Effective distractors need to be about three times as strong in distributed WM networks compared to localized WM networks.
claims.source: Overall, we found that localized WM networks can be distracted with stimuli similar or even weaker than the minimum cue input strength required to encode a WM pattern, while effective distractors need to be about three times as strong in the case of distributed WM networks (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The difference in distractor robustness is due to the robustness of a distributed attractor and the effect of counterstream inhibitory bias.
claims.source: This difference is due to the robustness of a distributed attractor compared to a local circuit mechanism, but also to the effect of the counterstream inhibitory bias which dampens the propagation of distractor signals (cf. MT responses in Figure 8B and C).

claims.claim: The model predicts a positive correlation between the number of areas involved in a WM task and their average firing rate of sustained activity.
claims.source: First, the model predicts a positive correlation between the number of areas involved in a WM task and their average firing rate of sustained activity (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimentally testable prediction.

claims.source: Third, distributed WM is significantly more robust to distractors than localized WM (Figure 8), due to their intrinsic resilience and the inhibitory feedback condition.

claims.source: Fourth, electrophysiological recordings in macaques could test whether FEF areas require support from frontal areas (in the form of strong excitation) to maintain WM-related activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

results.result: The authors developed an anatomically constrained computational model of 30 macaque cortical areas with inter-areal connectivity based on tract-tracing data, incorporating a gradient of synaptic excitation along the cortical hierarchy based on dendritic spine counts, and assuming graded feedforward excitatory and feedback inhibitory projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 describe the model architecture with clear references to anatomical data sources (Markov et al., Elston et al.) and explicit figures showing the implementation. The model constraints are well-documented in both text and supplementary materials, providing a solid foundation for subsequent analyses.

results.result: The model demonstrates that mnemonic internal states can emerge from inter-areal reverberation even when isolated areas cannot generate self-sustained activity, producing distributed sustained activity patterns across frontal, temporal, and parietal areas that agree with experimental evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C18-C22, and C24 collectively demonstrate the core distributed WM mechanism through simulation results (Figure 2). The model produces sustained activity patterns matching meta-analyses of experimental data (C20), with stimulus-specific selectivity (C21) and area-specific dynamics (C22). The spatial transition in firing rates (C24) provides a novel theoretical prediction.

results.result: The model reveals a novel spatial transition separating cortical areas engaged in working memory from those that are not, which is robust to different ranking methods and does not require parameter fine-tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C25-C27 describe the spatial transition phenomenon shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures. The transition appears consistently across different ranking methods (C26, Figure 2—supplement 5) and is characterized as robust (C27), representing a novel theoretical insight distinct from classical bifurcation theory.

results.result: A simplified model demonstrates that distributed WM patterns can emerge in generic networks of excitatory units with a linear gradient of local couplings when long-range connections are sufficiently strong, even when isolated nodes cannot generate bistability.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 describe the simplified model analysis (Figure 3A-D) with mean-field analytical solutions confirming the mechanism. The mathematical framework provides theoretical support for the distributed WM concept, showing it requires minimal ingredients (strong inter-areal connections and a gradient of local properties).

results.result: When biological constraints are considered (saturating spine count gradient), the model requires asymmetric feedforward/feedback projections (counterstream inhibitory bias) to produce realistic distributed WM patterns involving only a subset of areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 demonstrate through the simplified model (Figure 3E-F) that saturating gradients prevent distributed WM unless feedback projections are weaker than feedforward ones. This provides theoretical justification for the CIB hypothesis and links model requirements to biological data.

results.result: Counterstream inhibitory bias (CIB) prevents indiscriminate sustained activation across all cortical areas, reduces firing in early sensory areas while maintaining appropriate activity in higher areas, and allows distributed WM patterns to emerge across a wide range of coupling strengths with moderate to strong CIB agreeing well with experimental evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C37-C40 describe the CIB mechanism and its effects (Figure 4). The systematic variation of CIB strength (C38-C39) demonstrates its functional role, and comparison with experimental evidence (C40, Figure 4D) provides validation. The mechanism is both theoretically motivated and empirically supported.

results.result: The large-scale circuit displays a large number of distinct distributed sustained activity attractors defined by their spatial patterns, with the number of attractors showing an inverted-U relationship with global coupling strength. A positive correlation exists between attractor size and mean firing rate, and attractor composition depends on the number of intrinsically multistable areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46, C71-C72 describe the diversity of attractors (Figure 5). The systematic exploration across different parameter regimes (C43, C45-C46) and the correlation analysis (C44) provide comprehensive characterization. The finding that many attractors are not accessible from sensory stimulation (C72) has important functional implications.

results.result: Distributed WM attractors show resilience to area inactivation, with the number of active areas and their firing rates decreasing only linearly with random inactivations. Silencing areas in the anatomical 'bowtie hub' has stronger impact than peripheral areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C50 demonstrate robustness through systematic inactivation studies (Figure 6A-B, F-G). The linear degradation (C47-C48) contrasts with catastrophic failure and the bowtie hub analysis (C50) links network topology to functional resilience, providing testable predictions.

results.result: Prefrontal areas control distributed attractors: inactivating dlPFC prevents distributed WM emergence in strongly distributed networks, brief inactivations in distributed WM allow information recovery (unlike localized WM), and distributed attractors can be deactivated by targeting inhibitory populations in a small set of frontal areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C51-C57 demonstrate prefrontal control mechanisms (Figure 7). The comparison between localized and distributed WM (C53-C54) provides clear predictions, and the selective shutdown mechanism (C55-C57) shows how distributed patterns can be controlled from specific nodes despite their spatial extent.

results.result: Distributed WM is significantly more robust to distractors than localized WM, requiring distractors approximately three times stronger to disrupt memory maintenance, due to both the intrinsic resilience of distributed attractors and the dampening effect of counterstream inhibitory bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C58-C60, C63 demonstrate distractor robustness through systematic comparison (Figure 8). The quantitative difference (3x stronger distractors needed, C59) and mechanistic explanation (C60) linking to CIB provide both empirical and theoretical support for this prediction.

results.result: The model generates four experimentally testable predictions: (1) positive correlation between number of areas involved and their firing rates, (2) brief silencing of areas in distributed WM allows information recovery, (3) distributed WM is more robust to distractors, and (4) FEF areas require frontal support for WM activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62, C64 explicitly state testable predictions derived from the model. These are clearly distinguished from the model results themselves and provide concrete experimental approaches to validate the distributed WM framework. Each prediction has clear empirical implications.

results.result: The distributed WM mechanism requires minimal elements and is likely to generalize to other species (rodents, humans), with CIB being a plausible condition as long as local property gradients grow sublinearly.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 discuss generalizability based on the simplified model (C66) and theoretical considerations (C67). While the minimal requirements suggest broad applicability, actual validation in other species requires empirical testing. The claims are speculative but theoretically grounded.

results.result: The model provides a novel theoretical framework showing that graded circuit properties along the cortical hierarchy can explain qualitatively distinct functions of different areas through a spatial transition that cannot be simply explained by parameter gradients, potentially exhibiting dynamical criticality.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 articulate the theoretical contributions. The spatial transition mechanism (C69) represents a novel form of bifurcation in networked systems, and the prediction of dynamical criticality (C70) follows logically from the transition phenomenon, though C70 remains speculative pending experimental validation.

results.result: Distributed attractor states could serve various forms of internal representations not triggered by particular sensory pathways or encoded differently as memories.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 speculates about functional roles of non-sensory-accessible attractors. While the existence of such attractors is demonstrated (C72), their specific functional roles remain hypothetical. This represents an interesting direction for future work but lacks direct support.

results.result: Working memory has traditionally been associated with localized frontal activity and local circuit mechanisms, but recent evidence shows distributed coactivation across multiple regions, which previous modeling efforts limited to two areas have not adequately addressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C10 establish the scientific context through citations to prior work. These background claims are well-supported by the cited literature and accurately represent the state of the field, motivating the need for large-scale distributed modeling approaches.

results.result: Population-level ramping activity of LIP in the model corresponds to trial-averaged temporal accumulation of information in decision-making.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 interprets LIP ramping activity by analogy to decision-making literature. While the model produces ramping (C22), the specific interpretation as decision-related accumulation is speculative and not directly tested. The connection requires additional validation.
